documents: Kaushal et al. 2022, Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems 23, e2022GC010529 (published paper, PDF, 16 pages)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (article pages 'n of 16'); supplementary pages not supplied

entry.evidence: It is therefore necessary to find a paleoproxy to reconstruct terrigenous dissolved organic matter (tDOM) parameters.

sequences.source_document: Kaushal et al. 2022, G-cubed, published paper

steps.action: The authors pose the problem that long tDOC and CDOM records are lacking outside Europe and North America and before the satellite era, so a paleoproxy is needed.
steps.quote: It is therefore necessary to find a paleoproxy to reconstruct terrigenous dissolved organic matter (tDOM) parameters.

steps.action: They take from their own and others' earlier work the mechanism that coral luminescence comes from incorporated humic-like substances, with the G/B ratio normalizing for skeletal structure.
steps.quote: The luminescence is caused by the incorporation of humic-like substances into the coral skeleton during growth

steps.action: They cite their earlier Borneo (Talang) calibration showing that G/B tracks satellite-derived aCDOM(440), and note that a single-wavelength proxy gives limited insight.
steps.quote: we recently showed that luminescence G/B in a coral from Borneo, extending back to 2002, tracks sub-annual terrigenous CDOM variability

steps.action: They state the working hypothesis that coral G/B is a quantitative proxy for tDOC concentration and for the full CDOM absorption spectrum.
steps.quote: coral luminescence G/B can be used as a quantitative proxy to estimate tDOC concentration

steps.action: They choose the Singapore Strait (Kusu Island), where monsoon current reversals naturally bring strong seasonal tDOC pulses from Sumatran peatlands.
steps.quote: The seasonally reversing currents thus result in seasonally high concentrations of tDOC and terrigenous CDOM in the Singapore Strait

steps.action: They use the monthly seawater time series (salinity, temperature, CDOM spectra, DOC, δ13CDOC) at Kusu, collected and published earlier by the same group (Zhou et al. 2021; Martin et al. 2021), averaged monthly.
steps.quote: Biogeochemical sampling was conducted at Kusu once or twice per month at 5 m depth from October 2017 to November 2020.

steps.action: They take the tDOC concentrations estimated by Zhou et al. (2021) with a two-endmember δ13C mixing model (peatland −29‰, marine −21.88‰).
steps.quote: Zhou et al. (2021) used a two-endmember mixing model to estimate the concentration of tDOC

steps.action: They collect two Porites plug cores (KU-K, KU-L), clean them, and measure luminescence G/B by UV spectral line scanning at about 0.07 mm resolution, with Sr/Ca and δ18O drilled alongside.
steps.quote: One plug core was collected from the main growth axis of each two massive Porites spp. corals (KU-K and KU-L)

steps.action: They build age-depth models by peak-aligning the 2018 and 2019 SW monsoon peaks in measured aCDOM(350) with G/B peaks, which gives growth rates of 16 and 10 mm/yr.
steps.quote: QAnalySeries software was used to peak-align the 2018 and 2019 SW monsoon peaks

steps.action: They check the age models independently by comparing measured temperature and salinity with coral Sr/Ca and δ18O (Supp. Figure 2).
steps.quote: which provides additional, independent validation of our age model

steps.action: They correlate G/B from both replicate cores with bulk DOC (poor), δ13CDOC and calculated tDOC (R = 0.64 and 0.90).
steps.quote: Coral G/B instead correlated well with δ13CDOC (KU-K R = −0.60; KU-L R = −0.86; Figure 4b) and with calculated tDOC concentration

steps.action: They reject bulk DOC, including marine autochthonous DOC, as the signal G/B records, because G/B misses the NE monsoon bulk-DOC peak.
steps.quote: the coral G/B did not reflect the NE monsoon peak in bulk DOC

steps.action: They use the two linear regressions to reconstruct tDOC from G/B over October 2017 to February 2020, with an RMSE of ±6.3 μmol/kg, and infer a higher 2018 than 2019 SW monsoon peak.
steps.quote: this reconstruction has an RMSE of ±6.3 μmol kg−1

steps.action: They correlate G/B with CDOM absorption at every wavelength (R > 0.6 from 230 to 550 nm) and with aCDOM(350), SUVA254, S275–295 and the slope ratio.
steps.quote: coral G/B was strongly correlated (R > 0.6) with monthly average CDOM absorption at every wavelength between 230 and 550 nm

steps.action: They reconstruct SUVA254 from G/B by linear regression (RMSE ±0.34 L/mg/m).
steps.quote: coral G/B can also be used as a proxy to reconstruct SUVA254

steps.action: They reconstruct full CDOM spectra two ways: Method 1 fits an exponential through G/B-derived a300 and a400 and a zero at 700 nm; Method 2 uses G/B-derived a350 with the mean in-situ spectral slope.
steps.quote: We tested two methods for reconstructing the full CDOM absorption spectrum

steps.action: They compare the two spectrum-reconstruction methods by absolute and percentage RMSE against measured spectra at each wavelength (Figure 7; Figures S3–S5).
steps.quote: both methods provide similarly accurate reconstructions of the CDOM absorption spectrum

steps.action: They propose untested rival explanations for why G/B does not show the δ13C-implied NE monsoon tDOC: CDOM-poor or photobleached tDOC, weaker incorporation, or tDOC overestimated by the fixed endmembers.
steps.quote: It is also possible that tDOC during the NE monsoon was overestimated

steps.action: They invoke the published expectation that CDOM spectral slopes respond non-linearly to terrigenous mixing, to explain the weaker G/B–slope correlations.
steps.quote: CDOM spectral slope properties change in a strongly non-linear manner when tDOM mixes with low-CDOM marine DOM

steps.action: They refine the interpretation: G/B primarily traces absolute tDOM concentration rather than tDOM composition.
steps.quote: suggests that coral G/B primarily traces the variation in absolute tDOM concentration

steps.action: They prefer Method 1 for paleo-reconstruction because it has slightly lower RMSE and does not assume a constant past spectral slope.
steps.quote: Therefore, Method 1 provides a simpler approach for the reconstruction of CDOM.

steps.action: They compare the Kusu G/B–aCDOM(440) calibrations with the earlier satellite-based Talang (Borneo) calibration: slopes are indistinguishable, there is no significant interaction term, and there is a clear intercept offset.
steps.quote: the slopes of liner regressions are statistically indistinguishable since the standard errors (s.e.) of the slopes overlap

steps.action: They propose rival explanations for the site offset, colony differences versus site differences in a labile tDOM fraction, and leave them untested.
steps.quote: This might simply reflect individual differences between coral colonies

steps.action: They keep the claim that coral G/B is a calibrated quantitative proxy for monthly tDOC and CDOM, advising local calibration before use elsewhere.
steps.quote: Our study demonstrates that monthly resolution tDOC and CDOM variability in tropical coastal oceans can be reconstructed using coral cores.

tree.answer: Coral luminescence from incorporated humic-like tDOM; known from prior work
No; past tDOC is latent and must be inferred from coral G/B via calibration
Calibrate G/B as a quantitative proxy for tDOC, SUVA254 and CDOM spectra
G/B tracks bulk DOC vs tDOC; rival explanations for the NE-monsoon gap and the site offset
Bulk DOC would show an NE monsoon G/B peak; tDOC would not
Found: natural monsoon current reversal delivers seasonal peatland tDOC

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Yes: two SW monsoon seasons (2018, 2019) in two cores
Replicate cores, independent age-model check, two spectral methods, Talang slope comparison
Proxy kept with stated RMSE; local calibration advised
Not documented; review file not supplied (two anonymous reviewers thanked)

end.claim: Coral luminescence G/B is a quantitative proxy for tDOC concentration (RMSE ±6.3 μmol/kg), SUVA254 and the CDOM absorption spectrum from 230 to 550 nm in river-influenced tropical coastal seas.

decisive_move.sentence: Correlating G/B of two replicate cores against concurrent in-situ tDOC and CDOM parameters (R up to 0.90) is what turns a qualitative luminescence signal into a calibrated quantitative proxy.

gates.evidence: Action: the site and coral collection were chosen because the existing tDOC time series and strong monsoon seasonality suited proxy development (p. 9), so the proxy hypothesis directed the core collection; the water data were collected earlier for other aims (Zhou et al. 2021). Claim: the correlations could have failed, and the bulk-DOC correlation did fail; the Talang slope comparison could have shown differing slopes. However, the RMSE is computed on the calibration data, with no held-out period. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Isotope ratio mass spectrometry coupled to a TOC analyzer for δ13CDOC
UV line-scan camera with a dichroic RGB beam-splitter prism for spectral luminescence
Dual-beam UV-Vis spectrophotometry of CDOM absorption
Humic-like substances and aromaticity (SUVA254) as concepts linking terrestrial organic matter to fluorescence

novelty_claims.quote: we establish a method to study drivers of land–ocean tDOM fluxes and their ecological consequences in tropical coastal seas
we calibrate a method to reconstruct DOC records using luminescence measurements of coral cores

limits: Calibration spans about 2 years (two SW monsoons). The RMSE values are in-sample, with no held-out validation period; the Figure 4 caption gives the overlap period as January 2019 to February 2020 and a KU-L RMSE of 4.0, while the text gives a single ±6.3. The water data and the tDOC estimates are inherited from the authors' earlier papers, so the paper does not re-perform them. The claimed applicability over decades to centuries rests on cited persistence of luminescence, not on tests here. Rival explanations for the NE monsoon mismatch and for the Talang offset are stated but not tested. No review file was supplied, so review-driven changes are unknown; the acknowledgment says reviewers 'considerably improved' the manuscript. Sub-claims: SUVA254 and full-spectrum reconstruction are estimate_with_resolution (RMSE given); 'G/B primarily traces absolute tDOM concentration' is best_explanation; inferring relative CDOM variation without local calibration has no status (the authors say more cores are needed). Composition is coded natures_repetition because a relation is fitted across naturally repeated monsoon pulses without setting conditions; the headline claim is nonetheless a characterized capability (inference).

disagreements.target: Traditional use of coral luminescence as a hydroclimate (rainfall or runoff) proxy
disagreements.support: The paper shows G/B tracks tDOC and CDOM concentration quantitatively, recasting the signal as a biogeochemical tDOM proxy.
disagreements.quote: The resulting coral skeletal luminescence variability has traditionally been used to reconstruct hydroclimate variation.

disagreements.support: The authors extend the calibration to tDOC, SUVA254 and full spectra, and find a site-specific offset but a similar slope.
disagreements.quote: reconstructing just CDOM absorption at a single wavelength from a coral core can only give limited insights into land–ocean carbon flux dynamics

disagreements.target: Zhou et al. (2021) tDOC estimates during the NE monsoon (fixed endmembers)
disagreements.support: Negative tDOC values and the wide range of marine δ13C (Verwega et al. 2021) suggest a fixed marine endmember may bias NE monsoon tDOC.
disagreements.quote: It is also possible that tDOC during the NE monsoon was overestimated, since it was calculated using a fixed value for the marine endmember δ13CDOC

disagreements.target: Use of CDOM spectral slope ratios as tDOM tracers (Fichot & Benner 2011; Vantrepotte et al. 2015)
disagreements.support: Slopes did not distinguish the 2018 and 2019 monsoons, consistent with non-linear mixing behaviour (Stedmon & Markager 2003).
disagreements.quote: slope ratios might not be ideal measures of absolute concentration of tDOM and tDOC unless the terrigenous contribution is relatively low

alternatives_considered.chosen: Method 1 (exponential fit through G/B-derived a300, a400 and zero at 700 nm)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Method 2 (G/B-derived a350 with the mean in-situ spectral slope 300–550 nm)
alternatives_considered.reason: Slightly lower RMSE; the past spectral slope may have varied, so Method 2 may add uncertainty

alternatives_considered.chosen: aCDOM(350) as the seasonal tie-point for peak-aligning the age model
alternatives_considered.reason: aCDOM(350) provides a less ambiguous seasonal marker

alternatives_considered.chosen: Monthly averaged water measurements for comparison with coral data
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Higher-resolution individual aCDOM(350) data (used only for the age model)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Single fixed marine δ13CDOC endmember (−21.88‰) inherited from Zhou et al. (2021)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: A range of marine δ13C values (Verwega et al. 2021)
alternatives_considered.reason: none given (inherited); acknowledged to produce negative tDOC values in March and April 2019
